questions.question_text:
The array has complete rows of $4$ and one incomplete row. Which division statement does it model?
$\begin{array}{cccc}\bullet&\bullet&\bullet&\bullet\\\bullet&\bullet&\bullet&\bullet\\\bullet&\bullet&\bullet&\bullet\\\bullet&\bullet&&\end{array}$

options.why: Counted only two complete rows and left a remainder larger than the divisor.
Used the number of complete rows as the divisor instead of the row size.
Counted the incomplete row as a fourth complete group.

questions.question_text: Seventeen counters are shared equally among $4$ groups. Which description matches the model?

options.why: Stopped sharing one counter too early, leaving enough counters to add one to every group.
Used the number of groups as the remainder instead of counting the single leftover.
Placed too many counters in each group, so the proposed total is twenty-two rather than seventeen.

questions.solution_text:
$17=4\times4+1$
Each group has $4$ counters, with $1$ left over.

questions.question_text: A model has $6$ complete groups of $3$ counters and $2$ leftovers. How many counters are modelled?

options.why: Counted the counters in the six complete groups but omitted the two leftovers.
Added the group count, group size and remainder instead of multiplying the equal groups first.
Added the remainder to the group size before multiplying, treating every group as having five counters.

questions.question_text: Which model is valid for division by $5$?

options.why: A remainder of five makes another complete group, so it cannot be left over after division by five.
A remainder of eight is larger than the divisor, so another complete group can be formed.
A remainder of six is not less than the divisor five.

questions.solution_text: The valid model has $7$ full groups and $4$ leftovers because $4<5$.

questions.question_text: A partially filled array for $31\div7$ has how many complete rows and how many counters in its last row?

options.why: Stopped after three rows even though seven of the ten leftovers make another complete row.
Made five full rows of seven, which already uses more than thirty-one counters.
Used the divisor as the remainder instead of subtracting twenty-eight from thirty-one.

questions.solution_text:
$31=7\times4+3$
The array has $4$ complete rows and $3$ counters in its last row.

questions.question_text: A student models $38\div9$ with $3$ full rows and $11$ leftovers. Which repaired model uses all $38$ counters?

options.why: Reduced the leftovers to $2$ but forgot to add the extra complete row, so the model holds only $29$ counters.
Moved a row of ten out of the $11$ leftovers instead of a row of nine, so the model holds only $37$ counters.
Moved a row of ten out of the leftovers and also forgot to add the extra complete row, leaving just $28$ counters.

questions.solution_text:
$11=9+2$
$38=9\times4+2$
The repaired model has $4$ full rows and $2$ leftovers.
